42863651.label: Background
42863651.text: Cardiac imaging with positron emission tomography and computed tomography (PET/CT) is a principal technique in the diagnosis and prognostication of coronary artery disease. PET/CT image quality can be negatively impacted by patient, cardiac, and respiratory motion.

42863651.label: Methods
42863651.text: We evaluated images from 102 patients clinically referred for cardiac rest/stress Rb-82 PET/CT myocardial perfusion imaging. Patient images were processed with a prototype data-driven motion detection algorithm and stratified by motion severity. Images were subjected to cardiac (CardioFreeze single [CS]) or cardiac and respiratory (CardioFreeze dual [CD]) motion correction via a novel reconstruction tool. Validated image quality markers including target-to-background ratio (TBR), were assessed between corrected and non-corrected images and analyzed via student's t-tests.

42863651.label: Results
42863651.text: The motion detection algorithm identified 36 (35.3%) patients with significant motion. Image processing via CS yielded a statistically significant increase in mean image contrast (TBR 3.65 ± 0.07, P < 0.01) and this effect intensified when respiratory motion correction was applied (3.78 ± 0.07, P < 0.005). Motion correction is more effective when applied to images containing greater motion, improving mean TBR by 3% (P < 0.05) in non-motion scans but by greater than 10% (P < 0.01) in significant motion cases. Three months post-imaging, 18 patients underwent clinically indicated coronary angiography: seven patients demonstrated significant motion, and CD motion correction improved their image quality to that of patients with no motion.

42863651.label: Conclusions
42863651.text: Over 1/3 of patients undergoing cardiac PET/CT have detectable motion leading to potential artifacts with clinical significance. Cardiac and respiratory motion correction improves image quality and may improve diagnostic accuracy, particularly when respiratory motion is severe. Further studies are critical to investigate the clinical impacts of improved image quality.

42895551.label: Background
42895551.text: Yttrium-90 transarterial radioembolization (TARE) combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors has been investigated as a potential therapeutic strategy for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, evidence supporting its addition to current standard systemic therapy remains limited. We aimed to compare clinical outcomes in patients with advanced HCC treated with TARE followed by atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (TARE-Atezo/Bev) and Atezo/Bev alone.

42895551.label: Materials and methods
42895551.text: This retrospective cohort study included systemic therapy-naïve patients with advanced HCC treated with Atezo/Bev alone or TARE-Atezo/Bev at a single tertiary hospital between 2018 and 2025. Baseline characteristics were adjusted using propensity score matching (PSM) and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), and the secondary outcome was progression-free survival (PFS).

42895551.label: Results
42895551.text: A total of 156 eligible patients were enrolled, including 93 in the Atezo/Bev group and 63 in the TARE-Atezo/Bev group. In the unmatched cohort, median OS was significantly longer in the TARE-Atezo/Bev group than in the Atezo/Bev group (14.1 vs 6.4 months; hazard ratio=0.43, 95% confidence interval = 0.29-0.63; p < 0.001), with consistent results after PSM (p = 0.01) and IPTW (p < 0.001). Although PFS was comparable between groups in the overall cohort, patients with Child-Pugh class A (OS: 14.6 vs 7.1 months; PFS: 7.7 vs 6.3 months) or ALBI grade 1 (OS: 21.4 vs 8.3 months; PFS: 8.1 vs 5.7 months) had significantly longer OS and PFS in the TARE-Atezo/Bev group, with similar results after adjustment.

42895551.label: Conclusions
42895551.text: Sequential TARE-Atezo/Bev may improve survival compared with Atezo/Bev alone in patients with advanced HCC and well-preserved liver function.

42895551.label: Key points
42895551.text: QuestionThe survival benefit of yttrium-90 TARE followed by Atezo/Bev compared with Atezo/Bev alone remains uncertain given limited evidence in advanced HCC. FindingsTARE followed by Atezo/Bev was associated with significantly longer OS than Atezo/Bev alone, with both OS and PFS improved in patients with advanced HCC and preserved liver function. Clinical relevanceSequential TARE followed by Atezo/Bev may offer a survival advantage in selected patients with advanced HCC, supporting the integration of locoregional and systemic therapies.

42912551.text: We report a case of a 60-year-old man with biopsy-proven prostate adenocarcinoma who underwent 99m Tc-PSMA scintigraphy during evaluation for potential 177 Lu-PSMA radioligand therapy. The scan demonstrated diffuse skeletal radiotracer accumulation resembling a bone scan. A focal photopenic defect in the thoracic spine corresponded on SPECT/CT to a vertebral hemangioma of the T9 body. An elongated, ventrally deviated (hook-like) xiphoid process, considered a benign anatomic variant, was also identified. This case underscores the importance of recognizing atypical 99m Tc-PSMA distribution patterns and correlating functional with anatomic imaging to avoid misinterpretation and optimize diagnostic accuracy.

42933251.text: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) are characterized histologically by an inner mucin-producing columnar epithelium supported by a dense ovarian-type stroma. MCNs account for approximately 10% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice, as MCNs may harbor high-grade dysplasia or progress to invasive carcinoma. Establishing reliable imaging criteria for risk stratification is critical to identify patients who are candidates for surgery. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging play pivotal roles in lesion characterization and assessment of features associated with high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Current guidelines recognize several imaging features as high-risk characteristics for MCNs, including large tumor size, mural nodules, and main pancreatic duct dilatation. However, other potential predictors of malignancy remain poorly defined and are not sufficiently emphasized. The strongest MCN-specific evidence, as demonstrated in multivariable analyses, supports larger cyst size, mural nodules, main pancreatic duct dilatation, and, in selected cohorts, elevated serum cancer antigen 19-9. Male sex has also been associated with malignancy in retrospective surgical cohorts, whereas pancreatic head/neck location, calcification, wall/septal thickening, age, and signal heterogeneity on T2-weighted images remain less consistently validated. Importantly, most malignancy-prediction literature is based on resected, pathologically confirmed MCNs and is therefore vulnerable to selection and verification bias and cannot be directly extrapolated to all incidentally detected presumed MCNs. This article presents a transparent literature search methodology and an evidence-based synthesis of predictors of malignancy that clearly distinguishes MCN-specific multivariable evidence from lower-level or extrapolated data. It also provides a comparison of key guidelines. Unlike previous reviews, this article directly addresses the evidence gap between resection-based cohorts and the broader population of incidentally detected presumed MCNs. It also clarifies when imaging findings should prompt further evaluation rather than independently determine management.

42957801.label: Objectives
42957801.text: To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text.

42957801.label: Materials and methods
42957801.text: In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections (n = 359) and conclusion sections (n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch-Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t-tests.

42957801.label: Results
42957801.text: Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1-Q3 5-5] vs 4 [3-5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5-5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48-84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%).

42957801.label: Conclusion
42957801.text: A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation.

42957801.label: Key points
42957801.text: Question Can a locally hosted LLM generate patient-friendly radiology reports while preserving data privacy and maintaining acceptable accuracy, completeness, and readability? Findings A locally hosted LLM generated patient-friendly report conclusions with higher quality scores than main reports, while clinically relevant hallucinations remained an important safety concern. Clinical relevance A locally hosted LLM has potential to generate patient-friendly radiology report translations without external cloud data transfer. Report conclusions appear to be the most promising initial application, although clinician oversight and further patient-centered validation remain essential before clinical implementation.

42975301.text: Background Contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) is increasingly used in breast cancer diagnostics; however, randomized trials assessing the added value of CEM in preoperative staging of breast cancer beyond digital mammography, digital breast tomosynthesis, and US are lacking. Purpose To assess the added value of CEM for preoperative breast cancer staging in a randomized controlled trial. Materials and Methods This prospective randomized controlled trial (Added Value of Preoperative Contrast Enhanced Mammography in Staging of Malignant Breast Lesions) enrolled women diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer eligible for primary surgery at two breast centers in Sweden. Participants were randomized 1:1 to preoperative CEM or control from November 2020 through April 2024. The primary outcome was a 10% change in treatment due to preoperative CEM findings. Secondary outcomes included differences in reoperation and mastectomy rates between groups and accuracy of malignant extent estimation with CEM, mammography/tomosynthesis, and US using histopathologic extent as the reference, assessed with Bland-Altman statistics and concordance analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed according to menopausal status, breast density, histopathologic type of cancer, lesion size, and presence of microcalcifications at baseline imaging. Results In total, 415 participants (median age, 66 years; IQR, 56-73 years) completed the trial: 202 in the CEM group and 213 in the control group. Treatment was changed in 17 of 202 participants (8.4%; 95% CI: 5.3, 13.1) based on CEM findings. No evidence of differences was observed between the CEM and control groups with regard to mastectomy (17% [35 of 202] vs 18% [39 of 213]; P = .78) or reoperation (7.9% [16 of 202] vs 10% [22 of 213]; P = .39) rates. CEM showed the closest agreement with histopathologic malignant extent (bias, 3.5 mm), outperforming mammography and/or tomosynthesis (4.8 mm) and US (10.7 mm) overall and in nine of 10 predefined subgroups, except for ductal carcinoma in situ. Conclusion This trial did not meet its primary end point of a 10% treatment change; however, preoperative CEM improved malignant extent estimation.

42993301.text: Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is a minimally invasive treatment option for symptomatic patients with severe mitral valve disease who are at high surgical risk or ineligible for open-heart surgery. The procedure has been associated with improved quality of life and functional status in selected patients and is increasingly recognized as a valuable therapeutic option in the management of complex mitral valve disorders. A multidisciplinary Heart Team is essential to ensure the clinical success of TMVR, and imaging specialists play a central role in the preprocedural assessment for patient and device selection, during the procedure, to guide and monitor the implantation, and after the procedure, for follow-up and for the correct diagnosis of short- or long-term complications. Echocardiography is required for initial diagnosis, for assessment of valve hemodynamics, intraprocedural guidance and monitoring. However, a multimodality approach including CT and/or MRI is frequently needed to correctly manage the phase of preprocedural planning and the diagnosis of complications. This consensus document, developed by a working group of experts from the European Society of Cardiovascular Radiology (ESCR) and the North American Society for Cardiovascular Imaging (NASCI), provides evidence-based recommendations for CT and cardiac MRI acquisition and post-processing in procedural planning and postprocedural evaluation in patients undergoing TMVR. Emphasis is placed on the technical requirements and standardization of imaging protocols, which must account for the heterogeneity of imaging equipment used in clinical settings. The document also outlines recommendations for all necessary preprocedural measures to ensure consistency, accuracy, and effective communication among specialists. KEY POINTS: Question How can CT and MRI acquisition, measurement, and reporting for TMVR be standardized to support accurate procedural planning, device selection, and follow-up? Findings This expert consensus provides recommendations for standardized CT and MRI protocols, key measurements, and structured reporting throughout TMVR planning and follow-up. Clinical relevance CT and MRI assessment may improve patient selection, procedural planning, multidisciplinary communication, and detection of postprocedural complications, supporting safer and more consistent TMVR practice across centers.

43015151.label: Purpose
43015151.text: To assess the prognostic value of plaque burden based on CACS and SIS categories over CAD-RADS.

43015151.label: Methods
43015151.text: In this retrospective, single-center study, 2850 adults who underwent elective CCTA between 2016 and 2020 were screened. A total of 1818 patients were enrolled based on very low-to-intermediate pre-test risk, good image quality (Likert score ≥4), and ≥3 years of follow-up. Clinical data were collected, and CAD-RADS 2.0 with CACS-based plaque burden (CACS-P score) and SIS-based plaque burden (SIS-P score) was quantified. Prediction of 5-point MACE composite outcome (late unplanned coronary revascularization, non-fatal myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, hospitalization for angina, all-cause mortality) and 2-point MACE composite outcome (non-fatal myocardial infarction and all-cause mortality) was evaluated using survival analysis and multivariable models.

43015151.label: Results
43015151.text: During a median available follow-up of 62 months, 178/1818 patients (9.8%) experienced a 5-point MACE and 96/1818 (5.3%) experienced myocardial infarction/death within the fixed 36-month analysis horizon. Both CAD-RADS severity and plaque burden scores were associated with adverse outcomes. Integration of the CACS-based P-score identified revealed heterogeneity in risk estimates within CAD-RADS categories. For the primary endpoint, CAD-RADS 3/P0 showed HR point estimates of similar magnitude to those observed in CAD-RADS 4-5/P0 and CAD-RADS 4-5/P3-P4 (HR 15.95 [95% CI:3.95-64.36], HR 16.21 [3.23-81.31], and HR 14.13 [5.70-35.01], respectively). For myocardial infarction/death, CAD-RADS 2-3/P0 showed HR point estimates of similar magnitude to those observed in CAD-RADS 4-5/P1-P2. Conversely, SIS-P provided limited additional within category risk stratification.

43015151.label: Conclusions
43015151.text: CACS-based P score may refine risk stratification in patients with mild-to-moderate stenosis.
